title: Rayleigh Criterion for Resolution
short_intro: The Rayleigh criterion is a widely accepted geometric convention that defines the minimum resolvable limit of separation between two point sources of light. It states that two images are just resolved when the central maximum of the diffraction pattern of one source falls exactly over the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the other source.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of resolving power, Rayleigh's criterion condition for circular apertures and optical instruments like microscopes and telescopes, conceptual dependency on wavelength and aperture diameter.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Mathematical derivations of resolving power of telescopes, microscopes, and diffraction gratings, angular separation limits, and numerical problems involving Rayleigh's criterion.

prerequisites: Fraunhofer diffraction from a single slit and circular aperture
Formation of central maximum and secondary minima in diffraction patterns
Wave theory of light and superposition principle

concept_notes.heading: Physical Basis of Rayleigh Criterion
bullets: Due to diffraction, light from a point object does not converge to a point image, but forms a central bright disk (Airy disk) surrounded by alternating dark and bright rings.
When two point objects are very close, their diffraction patterns overlap, making it difficult to distinguish them as separate entities.

Rayleigh established a quantitative limit: two sources are resolvable if their angular or linear separation allows the intensity dip between their central maxima to drop to about 81% of the peak intensity.

concept_notes.heading: Resolving Power of a Telescope
bullets: The resolving power of a telescope is defined as the inverse of the smallest angular separation (dθ) between two distant point objects that can be resolved by the telescope.
Given by Rayleigh criterion for a circular aperture of diameter D, dθ = 1.22 λ / D.
Resolving power (RP) = 1 / dθ = D / (1.22 λ), showing that larger objective diameters improve angular resolution.

concept_notes.heading: Resolving Power of a Microscope
bullets: The resolving power of a microscope is defined as the inverse of the minimum linear distance (Δx) between two point objects that can be resolved.
Expressed by the Abbe-Rayleigh relation Δx = λ / (2 n sin θ), where n sin θ is the numerical aperture (NA).
Immersing the objective lens in a medium of high refractive index n (oil immersion) decreases λ in the medium, thereby increasing the resolving power.

concept_notes.heading: Resolving Power of a Diffraction Grating
bullets: According to Rayleigh criterion, two adjacent spectral wavelengths λ and λ + dλ are just resolved by a grating if the principal maximum of order n for wavelength λ+dλ coincides with the first minimum of the same order n for wavelength λ.
The resolving power in this case is given by R = λ / dλ = N n, where N is the total number of ruled lines on the grating and n is the order of the spectrum.
Higher orders and a greater number of illuminated lines yield finer spectral line separation capability.

derivations.title: Angular Resolution Limit for a Circular Aperture
derivations.conditions: Fraunhofer diffraction through a circular aperture of diameter D
steps: Write the condition for the first diffraction minimum for a circular aperture: sin θ = 1.22 (λ / D), where θ is the angle of diffraction.
Apply the Rayleigh criterion: the central maximum of the second source coincides with the first minimum of the first source, meaning the angular separation between the two sources equals θ.
Assume the angle θ is very small, so that sin θ ≈ θ (in radians).
Substitute the small angle approximation to obtain the limiting angle of resolution dθ.

derivations.title: Resolving Power of a Diffraction Grating
derivations.conditions: Normal incidence of light containing two close wavelengths λ and λ + dλ
steps: The position of the nth principal maximum for wavelength λ is given by the grating equation: a sin θ = n λ.
The position of the first minimum adjacent to this maximum occurs at a path difference of (λ / N) added to nλ, so a sin(θ + dθ) = n λ + (λ / N), where N is total lines.
Differentiating the grating equation gives a cos θ dθ = n dλ.
Equating the angular width of the principal maximum to the separation between the two peaks yields the resolving power formula.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity Distribution Curves for Rayleigh Criterion
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three curves: (1) Unresolved case where peaks are far apart, (2) Just resolved case where the central peak of one pattern sits on the first minimum of the other (81% intensity dip), (3) Completely unresolved single broad peak.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the visual limit of separation where the central dip allows distinct identification of two separate point sources.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in conceptual questions asking for the distinct intensity profile of 'just resolved' point sources.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Airy Disk Diffraction Pattern
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A circular central bright spot surrounded by concentric dark and bright rings with decreasing intensity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the realistic image of a point source formed by a lens with a circular aperture due to aperture diffraction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Basis for understanding why circular apertures use the 1.22 factor instead of 1.00.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the minimum angular separation of two point sources that can be resolved by a telescope with an objective lens diameter of 1.0 m, using light of wavelength 550 nm.
solution_steps: Identify given values: D = 1.0 m, lambda = 550 nm = 5.5 	imes 10^-7 m.
Use Rayleigh criterion formula for a telescope: d	heta = 1.22  rac{lambda}{D}.
Substitute values: d	heta = 1.22 	imes  rac{5.5 	imes 10^-7}{1.0}.
Calculate the result: d	heta = 6.71 	imes 10^-7 rad.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating 2 cm wide with 4000 lines per cm. Find the resolving power of the grating in the second order and the smallest wavelength difference dlambda that can be resolved near 600 nm.
solution_steps: Calculate total number of lines N: Grating width = 2 cm, lines per cm = 4000, so N = 2 	imes 4000 = 8000 lines.
Calculate resolving power R = N n = 8000 	imes 2 = 16000.
Use R = lambda / dlambda to find dlambda: dlambda = lambda / R = (600 	imes 10^-9 m) / 16000.
Compute final value: dlambda = 3.75 	imes 10^-11 m = 0.0375 nm.

solved_numericals.question: A microscope has an objective with a numerical aperture of 0.12. If light of wavelength 500 nm is used, what is the limit of resolution (minimum distance between two resolvable points)?
solution_steps: Identify the given values: NA = n sin	heta = 0.12, lambda = 500 nm = 5 	imes 10^-7 m.
Use the microscope resolution formula: Delta x =  rac{lambda}{2 n sin	heta} =  rac{lambda}{2 cdot NA}.
Substitute the values: Delta x =  rac{5 	imes 10^-7}{2 	imes 0.12}.
Calculate the final value: Delta x =  rac{5 	imes 10^-7}{0.24} = 2.083 	imes 10^-6 m.

assumptions_and_limitations.assumption: The Rayleigh criterion is an arbitrary convention based on visual perception and intensity contrast (81% dip), not an absolute physical cutoff.
assumptions_and_limitations.limitation: Two point sources with unequal intensities or under high signal-to-noise ratio conditions can sometimes be resolved even if they violate the strict Rayleigh criterion (super-resolution techniques).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Rayleigh criterion implies zero intensity at the exact midpoint between two resolved sources.
common_misconceptions.correct: There is a finite intensity dip of about 19% (leaving 81% peak intensity at the center) between the two overlapping central maxima.
common_misconceptions.why: Diffraction fringes overlap smoothly, meaning intensity is never completely zero in the central overlap region for just resolved sources.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Increasing the magnification of a telescope improves its resolution.
common_misconceptions.correct: Resolution depends solely on objective aperture diameter D and wavelength lambda, not on eyepiece magnification.
common_misconceptions.why: Magnification only enlarges the diffraction image without adding finer optical detail if the objective aperture cannot resolve it.

quick_revision: Telescope angular resolution: d	heta = 1.22 lambda / D
Microscope linear resolution: Delta x = lambda / (2 n sin	heta)
Grating resolving power: R = N n
Shorter wavelengths and larger apertures improve optical resolution.
